title: Is Your Non-Compete Worthless? Here's How to Fix It

 Is Your Non-Compete Worthless? Here's How to Fix It
Hi Sara,
Let’s talk about non-competes—a favorite topic for business owners, and one of the most misunderstood legal documents in existence. 
I see it all the time: non-competes that sound airtight but, when tested, are about as useful as a screen door on a submarine.
The Big Mistake Everyone’s Making
The question everyone asks is ‘is this even enforceable’? And the answer is usually at least partially yes. But the question people SHOULD be asking is ‘does this even help me’ and the answer to that is often ‘nope, not a bit.’
Most non-competes include a geographical restriction. They say something like:
“You can’t compete within 20 miles of this business location.”
That might have worked when businesses were local, and horse-drawn carriages were all the rage. But in 2024, when services are offered nationwide (hello, internet!), a 20-mile radius is laughably ineffective.
Why It Matters
If your clients are scattered across the country, what good is a non-compete that only covers a tiny local area? It’s a loophole big enough to drive a semi-truck through. And trust me, if a former employee or buyer wants to compete with you, they will drive through it.
How to Fix It
Your non-compete needs to reflect where your clients actually are. If your business operates nationwide, then your non-compete should restrict competitors from providing services to your client base, wherever they’re located. Of course, you do have to balance that against federal and state laws relating to enforceability which is where all the nuance comes in and is why lawyers still have a job.
Don’t Let Your Non-Compete Work Against You
Non-competes are meant to protect your business, not give you a false sense of security. If your current agreement isn’t built for the way your business operates today, it’s time for a rewrite.

To stronger (and smarter) agreements,
Sara Sharp
Deal Attorney, Partner
SK&S Law Group
